# What changes now {#sec-ch15}

Predictions about AI often turn out wrong, so this last chapter stays with three things: what this book has shown, what it suggests, and what nobody knows yet.

::: {.goals}
- See the decision layer as a separate part of an AI system.
- Understand why cheaper decisions can mean more work for people.
- Leave with a clear plan for your first decision.
:::

## A separate layer for decisions

For the last few years, the usual AI system has been one big model doing everything: reading, deciding, writing and using tools, all through text.

![Two ways to build an AI system. Left: one model does everything as text. Right: each layer does one job. An LLM reads and writes, a decision layer answers typed questions with probabilities, a policy turns those into actions, and tools, logs and people sit underneath.](/figures/ch29/stack.pdf){#fig-stack}

The right side of @fig-stack shows the design this book keeps reaching. The LLM does what only an LLM can do: read anything and write for people. The decision layer answers small, clear questions in one step, with probabilities we can test. The policy sets thresholds based on costs and team capacity. And at the bottom, tools take actions and people review. Each part is smaller than the whole system, can be tested on its own, and can be replaced without rebuilding everything else. This is the main reason this design is likely to last.

::: {.keyidea}
**Give each part one job.** The LLM reads and writes, the decision layer decides, the policy acts, and people own the costs.
:::

## Cheaper decisions, more decisions

In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons noticed something surprising about coal [@jevons1865]. James Watt's steam engine produced much more work from each tonne of coal. People expected Britain to use less coal. Instead, it used much more, because cheaper coal power was now used for many more things. We have seen the same with mobile data in India: when data became very cheap, people did not just save money; they started watching videos all day. This pattern is called the **Jevons paradox**. The name Jev comes from Jevons, and this time the "coal" is decisions.

A decision is worth making only when the loss it prevents is bigger than its cost, and when it can be made in time. A company makes a few thousand careful decisions per day, but it *could* make millions: one for every email, every login and every line in its logs. Each of these is worth only a tiny amount to check. At the example LLM price of \${{< num ch19 llm_price f5 >}} per decision, almost none are worth checking. At Jev's reported price of \${{< num ch19 jev_price f6 >}}, many are.

The interesting part is where the change shows up. For work a company already does, cheaper decisions mean many more decisions (in our example, {{< num ch19 decisions_ratio int >}} times more), but the total bill goes *down*. The bill goes up only when cheap decisions make *new* work worth doing, such as checking every file shared outside the company.

::: {.keyidea}
**Cheaper decisions create new work.** Like cheap mobile data, cheap decisions get used for many new things, and that is where the bill grows.
:::

![Alerts sent to a person per day, under two rules (illustrative). A rule that flags a fixed share of what the model looks at grows with the number of decisions, and at Jev volumes it sends far more than the team can handle. A cost-based threshold, which flags only when the expected loss is larger than the cost of a review, barely moves.](/figures/ch19/flags.pdf){#fig-flags}

There is a hidden cost: more decisions also means more cases sent to people. A rule that seemed fine at low volume, such as "send the top 0.1% to a person", sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_llm int >}} cases per day, within the team's capacity of {{< num ch19 capacity int >}}. At the new, higher volume, the same rule sends {{< num ch19 flags_top_jev int >}} per day, even though nobody changed it (@fig-flags). A cost-based rule, which sends a case only when its expected loss is higher than the cost of a review, sends {{< num ch19 flags_cost_jev int >}} per day in both cases.

::: {.keyidea}
**When volume grows, set thresholds by cost, not by percentage.** "Send the top 1% to people" grows with volume; "send it when the expected loss is more than the cost of a review" does not.
:::

## What becomes valuable

If deciding becomes cheap, what becomes rare and valuable? Good judgement about the decision itself. Someone still has to decide what each mistake costs, where the thresholds should be, how many cases the team can review, and whether the probabilities are still correct this week. No model can do this for you. This is why the first chapters of this book, about probability, calibration and costs, are the foundation. They are the difference between a system that makes a million cheap decisions well and one that makes a million cheap mistakes.

![Skills that matter more when decisions get cheap, and skills that matter less on their own, with the chapters that teach each.](/figures/ch29/skills.pdf){#fig-skills}

::: {.keyidea}
**Judgement is the skill that becomes valuable.** Someone must decide the costs, the thresholds and the team size. No model can do this for you.
:::

Many things are still unknown: how well any System One model is calibrated on your data, how it changes between versions, how it handles attackers, and what prices will finally be. None of these is a reason to wait. Calibration can be tested this week. Version changes can be handled with a fixed version and daily monitoring. Prices can be checked in a spreadsheet. And this design does not depend on any one company: a clear question in, a probability out, and a policy in your own code can be moved to a different model in a day.

![Open questions, and what you can do about each today.](/figures/ch29/unknowns.pdf){#fig-unknowns}

::: {.keyidea}
**Build so that you can measure, adjust and replace.** Measurable decisions, adjustable thresholds and a replaceable model keep you safe, whatever happens to any one company.
:::

## What to do on Monday

If you do only one thing after reading this book, make a list of every decision your system makes, and count how often each one happens. Most people are surprised by how many there are, and how many are small, clear and frequent.

![A first three months, one decision at a time.](/figures/ch29/monday.pdf){#fig-monday}

Then choose *one* decision. Collect a few hundred cases with known outcomes and test the calibration. Put a cost on each type of mistake and set the thresholds. Run it in shadow mode. Switch it on with a rule for failures, random checks and daily monitoring. Then move to the next decision. This is not exciting work, but it is how every system in this book became better.

::: {.breaks}
This chapter is the least certain part of the book. The cost and speed numbers are examples, and Jev's numbers are as reported by the company during early access. The idea that a separate decision layer will become standard is a reading of the evidence, not a proven fact. It could be wrong if general models become fast and well calibrated enough. Even then, everything about costs, thresholds and calibration will still apply.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Take the most frequent decision in your own system. What does a wrong "yes" cost? What does a wrong "no" cost? Where should the threshold be? And how will you know, one month from now, whether the probabilities behind it are still correct?

(There is no answer at the back of the book for this one. If you can answer all four questions, you have learned what this book set out to teach.)
:::

![The whole book as one story.](/figures/ch29/journey.pdf){#fig-journey}

Alan Turing ended his most famous paper with a line that suits this moment: "We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done" [@turing1950].

::: {.exercises}
1. Make a decision list for one system you know: every decision, how often it happens, what a mistake costs, and who is responsible for it.
:::

Thank you for reading.
:::
